report:
# Can Probiotics Lower Blood Sugar in Type 2 Diabetes?

**Short answer: Yes, modest evidence supports this—but effects are generally small and not universal across all trials.**

## The Evidence

Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) support a beneficial effect. A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs found probiotics significantly reduced HbA1c (SMD −0.38, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.14) and fasting insulin in type 2 diabetics ([PMC5491138](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5491138/)). A more recent 2024 systematic review confirmed probiotics "considerably reduce" HbA1c (MD −0.33, 95% CI −0.59 to −0.07), with effects even more pronounced for certain durations of intervention (6–8 weeks showed the strongest HbA1c improvement) ([PubMed 39114293](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39114293/)).

A specific probiotic formulation (Pendulum Glucose Control, containing *Akkermansia muciniphila* and other strains) was tested in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial and showed significant improvements in post-meal glucose control and reductions in A1C among people already on metformin ([PubMed 32675291](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32675291/)).

## Important Caveats

Not all trials agree. A 2025 randomized controlled trial found that probiotic supplementation did **not** lower HbA1c compared to placebo in T2D patients with suboptimal glycemic control ([ScienceDirect S2405457725003109](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405457725003109)), highlighting that results vary by probiotic strain, dose, and duration.

## Conclusion

The weight of meta-analytic evidence supports modest glucose-lowering effects of probiotics in type 2 diabetes, particularly for HbA1c and fasting insulin, though individual trial results are inconsistent and effects appear strain- and duration-dependent.
